title: Updating the Clinic Reminder System
text:
Harborview Clinic plans to revise the reminder messages it sends before appointments. Staff members began reviewing the system after noticing that missed appointments were especially common on Monday mornings. The clinic currently sends one text message at 6 p.m. the evening before each visit. Patients who do not use text messaging receive an automated phone call at the same time.

A three-week pilot tested an additional reminder on Friday afternoon for patients with Monday appointments. During the pilot, the number of missed Monday visits fell from an average of twenty-two per week to fifteen. Clinic managers caution that the pilot was short and that several other changes occurred at the same time. For example, reception staff also began confirming transportation needs for some older patients.

The clinic will continue the pilot for eight more weeks before deciding whether to use the extra reminder permanently. The scheduling team will track missed visits, canceled appointments, and the number of patients who ask to stop receiving messages. Staff members will also record whether patients report that the reminders are useful or excessive.

The revised public notice must explain the pilot without suggesting that the extra message has already been proven to solve the problem. It should also tell patients how to update their contact information and how to choose between text and phone reminders. Because the notice may be read quickly, the editor wants short sentences, clear transitions, and pronouns that refer to only one possible noun. The final version should sound professional while still being easy for patients to understand.

The communications team is also comparing the public notice with a shorter message used by a nearby clinic. Rather than copying that message, the team is studying which details patients need before they can act. Staff agreed that appointment dates, contact choices, and opt-out instructions should remain easy to locate. They also decided that statistics from the pilot belong in an internal report, not in a reminder that patients must scan quickly.

Before the notice is released, two staff members who did not help draft it will read it once without asking questions. They will mark any sentence that makes them stop to identify a pronoun, reread a condition, or guess whether a step is required. The editor will use those marks to make the final wording clearer without changing the clinic's actual policy.
